#### A join has two inputs, so it claims the minimum

**What is being answered.** Why a join is where the time decisions cost most — as the minimum rule and the pairing rule, side by side.

`joinWatermark(i)` has the line that matters: `if (w == NONE) { return NONE }`. A side that has produced nothing blocks the claim entirely, and a join has two sides by construction — so either one going quiet stops every result.

`matches(clock)` then shows the sharper cost. A mis-clocked aggregate puts a number in the wrong bucket; a mis-clocked join **pairs the wrong rows**, emitting an assertion that two things coincided. Step 4 compares the two pair sets from identical data.

The animation steps through the code, holding each line long enough to read the STACK (call frames and their locals) and the HEAP (allocated arrays and objects) as they are AT THAT MOMENT. Expand any step to study it on its own.

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch08-joins-memory/ch08-joins-memory.svg" alt="A join has two inputs, so it claims the minimum, 4 steps showing stack and heap" width="980">

<details>
<summary><b>Step 1 of 4</b> — a side that has produced nothing blocks the claim</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch08-joins-memory/frames/step-01.svg" alt="Step 1: a side that has produced nothing blocks the claim" width="980">

At row 0 only side "a" has produced anything, so `sideWatermark("b", 0)` is NONE and the join makes NO claim at all. A join is the case where this bites hardest: it has two inputs by construction, so either one being silent stops every result.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — and the claim is the lower of the two, never the higher</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch08-joins-memory/frames/step-02.svg" alt="Step 2: and the claim is the lower of the two, never the higher" width="980">

Side "a" has reached 480 and side "b" 200, so `lowest` ends at 200. Every join emission waits on whichever stream is further behind, however fast the other one is — which is ch03's propagation rule with the two inputs made structural.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — the clock decides WHICH ROWS ARE PAIRED</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch08-joins-memory/frames/step-03.svg" alt="Step 3: the clock decides WHICH ROWS ARE PAIRED" width="980">

`absDiff(1, 50)` = 49, within J = 60, so the pair is emitted. Note what this line asserts about the world: these two things happened close together. A wrong clock here does not mis-bucket a number, it states a false coincidence.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — so the same join on pt pairs a different set of rows</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch08-joins-memory/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: so the same join on pt pairs a different set of rows" width="980">

Compare the heap rows. Pairing on `et` and on `pt` gives different pair sets from identical data — id 7 arrived 230s after it happened, so on the arrival clock it sits next to rows it had nothing to do with. The output rows look equally plausible in both cases.

</details>
